glosses: passive of зацепи́ть (zacepítʹ)
потерять возможность движения, задев за что-либо

examples.text: — Извините, — сказала я холодно и хотела высвободить руку, но кру́жево рукава́ зацепилось за его пуговицу.
Проходя на своё место, халат её зацепился за что-то, она старательно, не торопясь, выпростала его и села.
Возможно, что сети зацепились за острые подводные скалы или железные обломки затонувших судов и порвались.
— Вот, пришли, входите сюда, тут за порог не зацепитесь, а то нос разобьёте.

glosses: схватить что-либо, схватиться за что-либо, чтобы не упасть, удержаться где-либо и т. п.

examples.text: Я кое-как надавил топор на снег, зацепился и повис; порыв ветра пронёсся.
Я же вёсла в лодку забрал, а сам концом верёвки зацепился и нетерпеливо жду, чтобы чуть Лука ногой в лодку ступит, сейчас плыть.

glosses: воен. остаться на какой-либо позиции; закрепиться

examples.text: После того как передовые батальоны зацепились за правый берег, были пущены в ход более совершенные приспособления и специальная понтонная техника.

glosses: перен., разг. использовать какую-либо возможность, чтобы остаться где-либо

examples.text: — Ох, худо больному старцу, — вздохнул он, — за что, кажись, только душа зацепилась, а всё держится, а всё свету рада.
Очень хотелось ей зацепиться в Газете, так что она вовсю старалась.
Отказали ей постольку поскольку там, в Америке, уже зацепился без визы её муж.

glosses: перен., разг. использовать что-либо как отправную точку для каких-либо размышлений или действий, как повод, предлог для развития мысли или для критики

examples.text: Он зацепился за эту мысль, ему казалось, что она может успокоить Машу.

translations.source_sense_description: потерять возможность движения, задев за что-либо

glosses: The act of seizing or capturing.

examples.text: The catch of the perpetrator was the product of a year of police work.

glosses: The act of catching an object in motion, especially a ball.

examples.text: The player made an impressive catch.
Nice catch!

glosses: The act of noticing, understanding or hearing.

examples.text: Good catch. I never would have remembered that.

"In that case," said Jeff, "I just thought of something else we need." He walked over to one of the stations that was selling household goods and bought a can opener.
"Nice catch," said Lucy.

glosses: The game of catching a ball.

examples.text: The kids love to play catch.

glosses: Something which is captured or caught.

examples.text: The fishermen took pictures of their catch.
The catch amounted to five tons of swordfish.

glosses: A find, in particular a boyfriend or girlfriend or prospective spouse.

examples.text: Did you see his latest catch?
He's a good catch.
"Aaaugh! Just once, I wish I could be considered a catch by men younger than fifty..."

glosses: A stopping mechanism, especially a clasp which stops something from opening.

examples.text: She installed a sturdy catch to keep her cabinets closed tight.

glosses: A hesitation in voice, caused by strong emotion.

examples.text: There was a catch in his voice when he spoke his father's name.

glosses: A concealed difficulty, especially in a deal or negotiation.

examples.text: It sounds like a great idea, but what's the catch?
Be careful, that's a catch question.

glosses: A crick; a sudden muscle pain during unaccustomed positioning when the muscle is in use.

examples.text: I bent over to see under the table and got a catch in my side.

glosses: A fragment of music or poetry.

examples.text: In the lightness of my heart I sang catches of songs as my horse gayly bore me along the well-remembered road.

"'Fair Enslaver!'" cried Mr. Enderby. "You must know 'Fair Enslaver:' there is not a sweeter catch than that. Come, Miss Ibbotson, begin; your sister will follow, and I—"
But it so happened that Miss Ibbotson had never heard 'Fair Enslaver.'

glosses: A state of readiness to capture or seize; an ambush.

examples.text: You lie at the catch again: this is not for edification.
The common and the canon law […] lie at catch, and wait advantages one against another.

glosses: A crop which has germinated and begun to grow.

examples.text: There was a good catch of rye and a good fall growth.

glosses: A type of strong boat, usually having two masts; a ketch.

examples.text: Fourteene miles Northward from the river Powhatan, is the river Pamaunke, which is navigable 60 or 70 myles, but with Catches and small Barkes 30 or 40 myles farther.

glosses: A type of humorous round in which the voices gradually catch up with one another; usually sung by men and often having bawdy lyrics.

examples.text: Let us be jocund: will you troll the catch / You taught me but while-ere?
One night, I remember, we sang a catch, written (words and music) by Orlo Williams, for three voices.

glosses: The refrain; a line or lines of a song which are repeated from verse to verse.

examples.text: The phrase repeated itself like the catch of a song.

glosses: The act of catching a hit ball before it reaches the ground, resulting in an out.

examples.text: It was he who removed Peter Bowler with the help of a good catch at third slip.

glosses: A player in respect of his catching ability; particularly one who catches well.

examples.text: […] in the field he is all activity, covers an immense amount of ground, and is a sure catch.

glosses: The first contact of an oar with the water.

examples.text: They are sitting up straighter, breaking their arms at the catch and getting on a terrific amount of power at the catch with each stroke.

glosses: A stoppage of breath, resembling a slight cough.

examples.text: When a Scot pronounces water, better, or bottle—wa’er, be’er, or bo’le—the sound is precisely that of the catch; […].
The glottal stop or glottal catch is the sound used in English in the informal words uh-huh 'yes' and uh-uh 'no'.

glosses: Passing opportunities seized; snatches.

examples.text: the way it has been writ in, by catches, and many long intervals of interruption

glosses: A slight remembrance; a trace.

examples.text: We retain a catch of those pretty stories.

glosses: To capture, overtake.
To capture or snare (someone or something which would rather escape).

examples.text: I hope I catch a fish.
He ran but we caught him at the exit.
The police caught the robber at a nearby casino.

glosses: To capture, overtake.
To entrap or trip up a person; to deceive.

examples.text: And they send unto him certain of the Pharisees and of the Herodians, to catch him in his words.

glosses: To capture, overtake.
To marry or enter into a similar relationship with.

examples.text: The public[…]said that Miss Bogardus was a suffragist because she had never caught a man; that she wanted something, but it wasn't the vote.
"She caught this blanquito guy from El Condado," and you immediately know "My god, all that money."

As for Aspasia, concubinage with Pericles brought her as much honor as she could hope to claim in Athens.[…]from the moment she caught her man, this influential, unconventional woman became a lightning rod[…].

glosses: To capture, overtake.
To reach (someone) with a strike, blow, weapon etc.

examples.text: If he catches you on the chin, you'll be on the mat.

The visitors started brightly and had an early chance when Valencia's experienced captain David Albeda gifted the ball to Fernando Torres, but the striker was caught by defender Adil Rami as he threatened to shoot.

glosses: To capture, overtake.
To overtake or catch up to; to be in time for.

examples.text: If you leave now you might catch him.
I would love to have dinner but I have to catch a plane.
Allen Gregory DeLongpre: Did anyone catch the Charlie Rose the evening before last. Did you catch it? No, nothing?

For reasons I shan’t bore you with, I got them to induce me at 39 weeks, at 10am, with the epidural going in first, and it was all a dream. […] But it was all over in time for my daughter to catch the Nigeria v Argentina World Cup game that evening, during which she seemed to reckon everything was miles offside.

glosses: To capture, overtake.
To unpleasantly discover unexpectedly; to unpleasantly surprise (someone doing something).

examples.text: He was caught on video robbing the bank.
He was caught in the act of stealing a biscuit.
Once he caught me gazing lingeringly and eagerly at him. He turned round with that mocking air he assumed when he wanted to hide his feelings.

glosses: To capture, overtake.
To travel by means of.

examples.text: catch the bus
The glare, the flies, while they waited, and he and the stationmaster put their heads together over the time-table, trying to find this other train, which, of course, they wouldn't catch.
After about a kilometer I caught a taxi to Santa Croce.

glosses: To capture, overtake.
To become pregnant. (Only in past tense or as participle.)

examples.text: Had Nancy got caught with a child? If so she would destroy her parent's dreams for her.

glosses: To seize hold of.
To grab, seize, take hold of.

examples.text: I caught her by the arm and turned her to face me.
Her aged Nourse, whose name was Glaucè hight, / Feeling her leape out of her loathed nest, / Betwixt her feeble armes her quickly keight […]

glosses: To seize hold of.
To take or replenish something necessary, such as breath or sleep.

examples.text: I have to stop for a moment and catch my breath
I caught some Z's on the train.

glosses: To seize hold of.
To grip or entangle.

examples.text: My leg was caught in a tree-root.

glosses: To seize hold of.
To be held back or impeded.

examples.text: Be careful your dress doesn't catch on that knob.
His voice caught when he came to his father's name.

Orion hit a rabbit once; but though sore wounded it got to the bury, and, struggling in, the arrow caught the side of the hole and was drawn out. Indeed, a nail filed sharp is not of much avail as an arrowhead; you must have it barbed, and that was a little beyond our skill.

glosses: To seize hold of.
To engage with some mechanism; to stick, to succeed in interacting with something or initiating some process.

examples.text: Push it in until it catches.
The engine finally caught and roared to life.

glosses: To seize hold of.
To have something be held back or impeded.

examples.text: I caught my heel on the threshold.

glosses: To seize hold of.
To make a grasping or snatching motion (at).

examples.text: He caught at the railing as he fell.

glosses: To seize hold of.
To spread or be conveyed to.

examples.text: The fire spread slowly until it caught the eaves of the barn.

glosses: To seize hold of.
To grip (the water) with one's oars at the beginning of the stroke.

examples.text: Stop gathering, in that gradual fashion, and catch the water sharply and decisively.

glosses: To seize hold of.
To germinate and set down roots.

examples.text: The seeds caught and grew.

glosses: To seize hold of.
To contact a wave in such a way that one can ride it back to shore.

examples.text: If you are surfing a wave through the rocks, make sure you have a clear route before catching the wave.

glosses: To seize hold of.
To handle an exception.

examples.text: When the program catches an exception, this is recorded in the log file.

glosses: To intercept.
To seize or intercept an object moving through the air (or, sometimes, some other medium).

examples.text: I will throw you the ball, and you catch it.
Watch me catch this raisin in my mouth.

glosses: To intercept.
To seize (an opportunity) when it occurs.

examples.text: she internally resolved henceforward to catch every opportunity of eyeing the hair and of satisfying herself,[…].

glosses: To intercept.
To end a player's innings by catching a hit ball before the first bounce.

examples.text: Townsend hit 29 before he was caught by Wilson.

glosses: To intercept.
To play (a specific period of time) as the catcher.

examples.text: He caught the last three innings.

glosses: To receive (by being in the way).
To be the victim of (something unpleasant, painful etc.).

examples.text: You're going to catch a beating if they find out.

glosses: To receive (by being in the way).
To be touched or affected by (something) through exposure.

examples.text: The sunlight caught the leaves and the trees turned to gold.
Her hair was caught by the light breeze.

glosses: To receive (by being in the way).
To become infected by (an illness).

examples.text: Everyone seems to be catching the flu this week.

glosses: To receive (by being in the way).
To spread by infection or similar means.

examples.text: Does the sedition catch from man to man?

He accosted Mrs. Browne very civilly, told her his wife was very ill, and said he was sadly troubled to get a white woman to nurse her: "For," said he, "Mrs. Simpson has set it abroad that her fever is catching."

glosses: To receive (by being in the way).
To receive or be affected by (wind, water, fire etc.).

examples.text: The bucket catches water from the downspout.
The trees caught quickly in the dry wind.
the sails caught and filled, and the boat jumped to life beneath us.

And the Bolshoi Ballet Academy’s account of the Grand Pas Classique from “Paquita” […] exemplified the spectacular czarist ideal of ballet that has long since became widely accepted as “classical ballet.” […] It catches an American athleticism and energetic team spirit that still seem to smash European notions of ballet classicism, as does its dancers’ selfless manner and their practicelike costumes.

glosses: To receive (by being in the way).
To acquire, as though by infection; to take on through sympathy or influence.

examples.text: She finally caught the mood of the occasion.
And the next thing I knew, I had caught feelings for her.

glosses: To receive (by being in the way).
To be hit by something.

examples.text: He caught a bullet in the back of the head last year.

glosses: To receive (by being in the way).
To serve well or poorly for catching, especially for catching fish.

examples.text: The nets caught well, and Mr. Deeley reported it the best fishing ground he ever tried.

glosses: To receive (by being in the way).
To get pregnant.

examples.text: Well, if you didn't catch this time, we'll have more fun trying again until you do.

glosses: To take in with one's senses or intellect.
To grasp mentally: perceive and understand.

examples.text: Did you catch his name?
Did you catch the way she looked at him?

“A tight little craft,” was Austin’s invariable comment on the matron;[…]. ¶ Near her wandered her husband, orientally bland, invariably affable, and from time to time squinting sideways, as usual, in the ever-renewed expectation that he might catch a glimpse of his stiff, retroussé moustache.

glosses: To take in with one's senses or intellect.
To take in; to watch or listen to (an entertainment).

examples.text: I have some free time tonight so I think I'll catch a movie.
Tom Holland: Gong Xi Fa Cai! It's Tom Holland here. // Mark Wahlberg: And I'm Mark Wahlberg. Catch us in Uncharted this Chinese New Year at GSC. // Tom Holland: Gong Xi Fa Cai!

glosses: To take in with one's senses or intellect.
To reproduce or echo a spirit or idea faithfully.

examples.text: You've really caught his determination in this sketch.

glosses: To seize attention, interest.
To charm or entrance.

examples.text: No, a far more natural beauty caught him.

glosses: To seize attention, interest.
To attract and hold (a faculty or organ of sense).

examples.text: He managed to catch her attention.
The enormous scarf did catch my eye.

glosses: To notice.

examples.text: -You made a typo. -Ah, thanks for catching that.

glosses: an etwas haken/festhaken

examples.text: Verdammt, mein Rock ist am Zaun hängengeblieben!
In der Nase sollen Verschmutzungen/Partikel der Luft hängenbleiben.
Eine Pistole muss ins Holster leicht herein- und wieder herausgleiten, bleibt sie hängen, dann taugt das Holster nichts.
[Strumflut 1962:] „Plötzlich machte der Fahrer mich auf eine Leiche aufmerksam, die an einer hohen Hecke hängengeblieben war, eine unbekleidete Frau mittleren Alters.“
„Man sollte hier keine Anhalter mitnehmen, denn die eingesetzten Drogenhunde erschnüffeln auch geringste Mengen, welche durch Abrieb von der Kleidung und den Händen an den Sitzen hängenbleiben.“
„Das Hinterland erreicht Höhen um 600 m, gerade genug, dass die Regenwolken regelmäßig hängenbleiben und abregnen.“

glosses: für etwas Negatives verantwortlich gemacht werden, als Auslöser/Verursacher für etwas Negatives gelten

examples.text: Für die Wahlniederlage ist der Spitzenkandidat verantwortlich, das wird eine Weile an ihm hängenbleiben.
„An Scholz bleibt in diesem Wahlkampf bisher nichts hängen.“

glosses: an einem Ort bleiben, verweilen

examples.text: Ich bin gestern abend in der Kneipe hängengeblieben, was habe ich heute für einen Kater!
Afrikanische Flüchtlinge bleiben häufig in Libyen in Lagern hängen.

[Wolfgang Ketterle, Physiker:] „»Ich bin als Post-Doc in die USA gegangen und habe dort eine wunderbare Stelle bekommen, und da bin ich heute noch. […] Wenn man auf Wanderschaft geht, dann kann man auch woanders hängenbleiben.«“

„Schon seit 2004 arbeitet Verena Issel als Bildhauerin und widmet sich immer wieder ausgefallenen Rauminstallationen. Damals kam die Norwegerin zum Studieren nach Hamburg. Blieb hängen, wie sie selbst sagt, und etablierte sich nach und nach in ihrer Sparte.“

„[…] dieser Notweg über den Walchensee soll offen sein und nicht gefährdet werden durch private Fahrzeuge, die da im Schnee hängenbleiben oder durch umstürzende Bäume. Wir versuchen, da möglichst wenige Fahrzeuge durchzulassen.“
„Das intelligente Schulbuch der Zukunft analysiert, wo Schüler beim Lesen hängenbleiben. Es kann folgern, ob Verständnisschwierigkeiten vorliegen.“

glosses: eine Klasse wiederholen müssen, nicht versetzt werden

examples.text: Ich bin in der 8. Klasse hängengeblieben und musste sie wiederholen.

glosses: sich etwas merken, etwas gelernt haben, im Gedächtnis bleiben

examples.text: Die Vokabeln, die ich mir gestern anschaute, habe ich heute schon wieder vergessen, sie sind nicht hängengeblieben.
Populisten setzen bewußt Lügen und Halbwahrheiten über ihre Kontrahenten in die Welt nach dem Motto: "Etwas wird schon hängenbleiben".
Von D. Trumps Unwahrheiten bleibt eine Menge bei seinen Anhängern hängen.

„Der Lkw-Fahrlehrer, der Grundschüler vorm toten Winkel warnt – […] Bei Fionn und Matthes ist auf jeden Fall schon eine ganze Menge hängengeblieben: »Vorher dachte ich immer, ein Lkw wäre wie ein Auto. Ich verhalte mich halt besser, halte mehr Abstand«, sagt Fionn.“

[Coronakrise 2020:] „Eine Videokonferenz [ersetzt] den Geschäftstermin, zu dem man morgens hinjettet und abends wieder zurück. Diese Erkenntnisse könnten hängenbleiben, auch nach der Krise, und dazu führen, dass Unternehmen sich stärker aufs Von-Zuhause-Arbeiten einstellen.“

[Fußball, der Spieler Bakery Jatta:] „Sein dynamischer Antritt und das starke Zweikampfverhalten und natürlich das sehenswerte Tor zum zwischenzeitlichen Ausgleich werden von diesem Pokalabend hängenbleiben, […].“
[Neuer Bischof Heiner Wilmer:] „Ein Zitat im ersten Jahr, das hängengeblieben ist: »Der Missbrauch von Macht steckt in der DNA der Kirche.« Heiner Wilmer hat damit viel Staub aufgewirbelt, […].“
